fullText:
speaking hypothetically
imagine you raise lots of money on the back of a whitepaper on fast-AI-take-off and deploy it into a combination of private AI plays and long-short leveraged public exposures
you grow, insanely and get to managing $120b gross on the public book.
further imagine you get caught out by a market-burble on your public book and force-liquidated out but are saved by the value of the private exposure which has gone vertical
even further imagine that the primary private exposure is lining up to IPO, talking to bankers, preparing to float.
you, the fund manager, want to you-know actually manage funds rather than simply sitting on a very valuable private exposure, and the bankers, now fully read in on and with a fairly decent sense of the value of your private exposure and line of site on the liquidity of the position are suddenly willing to accept some chunk--perhaps all--of your private exposure as collateral.
you reload.
(in the meantime many of the names that you previously were levered long on have rallied, but the whole trade is up-and-right in your view and so you put a lot of additional leverage on)
a small market burble. marginally less wildly crazy aggressive monetization flows through your private exposure (as measured quarter on quarter), crossed with some geopolitical uncertainty.
you're caught out again.
again!
as the book moves against you and moves against you again. as you grow increasingly desperate, hoping you can survive until the IPO or at least the s-1 listing, which will provide the market with more tangible evidence of the volume of end demand, you cover and cover, your equity against the underlying collateral getting whittled down and shaved off.
but it's too late for you.
too late.
(which is how, hypothetically, the entire market got wrong-footed on the liquidation of the same fund manager twice in the same year.)

fullText:
While I was writing this, my AI assistant got cut off by a bio safety filter. It was summarizing my own team's notes on the model we released today 😅

Frontier labs are moving fast into biology but the scientists and clinicians who'd get the most out of these models are unfortunately the ones running into walls like this one (and every day).

So we partnered with TIGEM (Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine), Naple "Federico II" University and Zhongguancun Academy to train Carbon-X.

Carbon-X is an open 14B model that reads raw DNA and talks about it in plain English. On our DNA benchmarks it scores 67%, vs 61% for Claude Opus 5.5 and 50% for Gemini 4 Argon, and its within a point of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 1000x lower cost.

We kept human and animal viruses out of the training data. The weights are open and the model runs on hardware accessible to academia (a laptop).

One example from the blog: give frontier models an 8kb stretch of the NF1 gene with a mutation at a splice site. Most of them call it benign, refuse, or run out of tokens. Carbon-X says pathogenic, because the mutation breaks the splice site.

This century, biology may be where AI matters most. We want to get there with the safety work done in the open and every lab in the world able to build on it. Go try it, and tell us what you find.

fullText:
// MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory //

Great insights for agent builders; bookmark it.

As models increase in capability, they also improve at things like memory generation.

Agent memory frameworks are everywhere right now. This study measured whether they still help once the model can search raw history itself.

The results suggest that a strong model needs less designed memory and
better tools for searching the raw record.

On one 419-turn LoCoMo conversation, Mem0 beats plain full context only with GPT-4o-mini. Building Mem0's memory costs more than an entire full-context rollout.

With Claude Opus 5.5, the Pi coding agent searching the raw history scores 99% for under half the cost of full context. Its one miss comes from a wrong answer key.

Memory also has a ceiling set by the model that wrote it. A stronger reader cannot recover what a weaker writer left out.

The author clearly defines the scope: one conversation and one run per cell. It is still a cheap experiment to repeat on your own agent before adding a memory layer.
